title: Rental renovation licensing program approved
subtitle: Also: OMERS reservist leave by-law, humane society contract, website launch, and a resident's CCTV presentation.
overview: Council approved a rental renovation licensing program aimed at "renovictions", where tenants are served N13 notices to vacate for renovations. Council did this {{vote:m9}} after rejecting the staff recommendation to keep the current level of service {{vote:m8}}. Landlords issuing an N13 would need a licence, with proof of a building permit and confirmation from a qualified professional. The program is funded from the Tax Rate Stabilization Reserve, and staff will bring the permanent funding request to the 2027 budget. Staff will also bring the by-law back for consideration.

Eviction decisions remain with the provincial Landlord and Tenant Board, and staff said the by-law would let the city lay charges for non-compliance but not stop an eviction. Many delegates asked for stronger measures, such as temporary accommodation and moving costs. Council also heard a resident's analysis of CCTV camera placement and a presentation on the new city website.

Council unanimously approved an OMERS by-law supporting reservist leave and a contract with the Humane Society of Kitchener Waterloo and Stratford Perth. A councillor also asked staff to remove strobing lights in Uptown.

decisions.detail: Council chose the licensing option with tenant supports, funded from the Tax Rate Stabilization Reserve, and directed staff to bring forward the by-law and a permanent 2027 budget request {{vote:m9}}.
A motion to keep the current service level and monitor renovation evictions, as staff recommended, failed {{vote:m8}}.
Council authorized the City to match OMERS contributions for employees buying broken service resulting from approved reservist leave.
Council authorized the Mayor and Clerk to sign an agreement with the Humane Society of Kitchener Waterloo and Stratford Perth, subject to the City Solicitor's satisfaction.

debate: Staff recommended keeping the current service level, citing a small number of N13 cases reaching the Landlord and Tenant Board over five years among about 21,000 rental units, and noting that the board alone decides evictions.

Delegates argued that the board data undercounts the problem because informal or uncontested notices are not tracked, and that a low number of licences would show the by-law is deterring renovictions. Several asked for temporary accommodation, rent top-ups and moving costs to be added.
Staff said the proposed positions reflect heavy complaint workloads for property standards officers. Delegates argued that Hamilton's costs suggest fewer staff would be needed.

Opponents on council said the matter is provincial jurisdiction, risks duplication, could drive evictions underground and adds to property taxes. Supporters said inaction abdicates responsibility to vulnerable residents and sends a message to bad-faith landlords.
One councillor sought to wait for Kitchener's consultant report. Others said the by-law could be amended later.
